Family Health

HRT for menopause: weighing benefits, risks and treatment choices

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Hormone replacement therapy, or HRT, can make troublesome menopause symptoms much easier to live with. It is also a prescription decision with several different forms and risk profiles. The useful question is what a particular treatment would do for you, considering your symptoms, age, medical history and preferences. A headline saying all hormones are dangerous (or that updated warnings mean there is no risk) cannot answer that question.

What menopausal hormone therapy replaces

During perimenopause, ovarian hormone production fluctuates; after menopause it is lower, rather than all oestrogen disappearing from the body. These changes can contribute to hot flushes, night sweats and genitourinary symptoms such as vaginal dryness or pain with sex. Symptoms vary and do not necessarily stop on a predictable date. New symptoms still need their own assessment.

HRT supplies oestrogen and, when needed, a progestogen. Progesterone is one kind of progestogen; other medicines have similar protective actions. Treatment may act throughout the body or mainly in vaginal tissues. It is not a general rejuvenation programme, a way to correct every hormone number, or a treatment for every illness that happens in midlife.

Age and time since menopause influence the decision

You can discuss treatment during perimenopause without waiting for periods to stop or symptoms to become unbearable. For suitable people younger than 60 or within about ten years after menopause begins, the balance is often favourable for bothersome symptoms. That describes a decision window, not a requirement to start ten years before menopause or a guarantee of safety.

Starting systemic HRT later can carry greater absolute risks and needs a careful individual discussion; continuing an effective treatment is a different decision from starting it for the first time. There is no automatic birthday on which everyone must stop. Premature ovarian insufficiency or early menopause needs a separate health and replacement plan, often continuing to the usual menopause age unless contraindicated.

Benefits are strongest when treatment matches the symptom

Systemic HRT is highly effective for hot flushes and night sweats. Better control of those symptoms may improve sleep and daily functioning. Low-dose vaginal oestrogen is a different option for local dryness, irritation and painful sex; it does not treat hot flushes. Vaginal moisturisers and lubricants can also help and may be used alongside prescribed local treatment.

Menopause-associated low mood may improve with appropriate HRT or menopause-specific cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), but diagnosed depression needs its own assessment and treatment. Hormones are not a substitute for psychotherapy or antidepressants when those are indicated. Sexual discomfort, urinary complaints or persistent poor sleep may also have causes requiring care beyond changing an HRT prescription.

Bones, muscles, the heart and the brain need different explanations

Systemic HRT can reduce bone loss and fragility fractures while it is being taken; protection decreases after stopping. Whether it is the appropriate bone treatment depends on age, fracture risk, other illnesses and alternatives. Adequate nutrition, suitable activity and fall prevention still matter. Evidence that HRT improves muscle mass or strength is limited, so it should not be promised to prevent all age-related muscle loss.

Do not start HRT solely to prevent cardiovascular disease or dementia. Possible associations with Alzheimer’s or Parkinson’s disease do not establish a prescription indication to prevent either condition. Hormones do not replace blood-pressure, cholesterol or diabetes care, or neurological assessment when needed. Studies suggesting benefits in particular groups cannot be turned into a guarantee of longer life or protection for every person.

The route and formulation matter

Systemic oestrogen can be supplied as tablets or through patches, gel or spray. Some markets also have injectable products with specific indications. Products differ in absorption, application, interactions and risks; injections, patches and tablets are not interchangeable doses. Use a regulated product and its instructions. A compounded or plant-derived product is not proven safer simply because it is called natural or bioidentical.

Low-dose vaginal creams, tablets, pessaries or rings mainly treat local symptoms, with much less systemic exposure. However, vaginal placement does not automatically mean local-only treatment: Estring and the systemic ring Femring have different purposes. Other selected genitourinary options include vaginal prasterone or oral ospemifene, a receptor-modulating medicine rather than ordinary oestrogen or progesterone replacement. Availability and suitability require a product-specific discussion.

Womb protection and treatment routines

If you have a uterus, systemic oestrogen generally needs an appropriate progestogen to protect the womb lining. It may be supplied in the same product, separately, or through a suitable levonorgestrel intrauterine system. After total hysterectomy, oestrogen alone is usually used; a specialist may advise differently in particular circumstances. Low-dose local vaginal oestrogen usually does not require added progestogen.

Sequential combined treatment gives progestogen for part of a cycle and may cause an expected withdrawal bleed; continuous combined treatment gives both hormones continuously. The choice depends partly on menstrual stage and the exact product. Some postmenopausal products instead combine oestrogen with bazedoxifene, a receptor modulator, under separate prescribing rules. Do not add, omit or substitute hormones yourself. HRT itself is not contraception.

Why older headlines and newer warning changes need context

The Women’s Health Initiative trials changed prescribing after reports in the early 2000s. They studied particular oral preparations in postmenopausal participants of different ages, many older than people first seeking symptom treatment. Those findings remain important, but they cannot provide an identical risk estimate for every current product, route or age group. Later analyses refine the discussion rather than proving that all earlier risks were imaginary.

In February 2026, the US FDA approved changes to the boxed warnings of six menopause hormone products following its 2025 request. This did not update every product simultaneously or erase all warnings: current systemic labels still contain contraindications and cardiovascular or cancer precautions, and systemic oestrogen-alone products retain the endometrial-cancer boxed warning. Read the current label for the actual medicine offered in your country.

Breast-cancer risk differs between regimens

Combined systemic HRT increases breast-cancer risk, with a larger increase after longer use. The risk declines after stopping but may remain above that of someone who never used it for years. Oestrogen-only treatment after total hysterectomy has very little or no increase according to NICE’s overall assessment; individual studies and formulations do not all give identical findings.

Ask about absolute risk over a stated period for people with a similar history, rather than comparing percentages with different timeframes. A patch is not automatically free of breast-cancer risk, and a bioidentical label does not establish protection. Previous breast cancer needs specialist discussion; systemic HRT is generally unsuitable, while persistent local symptoms may have different carefully considered options. Keep recommended breast screening up to date.

Endometrial and ovarian risks are separate

Unopposed systemic oestrogen increases endometrial-cancer risk when the uterus is present, including when delivered through the skin. Appropriate progestogen protection is therefore essential. The pattern and amount of protection matter: continuous and sequential regimens do not have identical bleeding or endometrial-risk profiles. Do not stop the protective part because bleeding is inconvenient without asking the prescriber.

Ovarian-cancer risk is low in absolute terms, but there is a very small increase with combined HRT and with longer use of oestrogen-only therapy. This is different from the womb-lining risk and cannot be removed simply by adding progesterone. Personal or inherited cancer history may change the discussion. Unexplained bleeding must be assessed rather than attributed automatically to treatment.

Blood clots, stroke and cardiovascular history

Oral systemic HRT raises venous blood-clot risk. Transdermal oestrogen generally has a lower clot-risk profile and is often considered when risk factors are present. Stroke risk also depends on age, dose and route; oral oestrogen can increase it, whereas it is unlikely to increase with transdermal oestrogen in the populations assessed by NICE. A lower-risk route does not mean every person with previous clots can use it without specialist assessment.

Smoking, age, prior clots, inherited clotting conditions, immobility, surgery, blood pressure and other illnesses belong in the consultation. A history of heart attack, stroke or significant cardiovascular disease may rule out a product or require an experienced specialist. HRT should not be chosen as a heart-protection medicine. Tell surgical teams about hormones well in advance; do not improvise a stopping or restarting schedule.

Gallbladder, liver and other health considerations

Oestrogen therapy can increase gallbladder-disease risk, particularly with oral preparations. Previous gallstones or gallbladder problems are reasons to review formulation and alternatives. Liver disease and severe triglyceride problems can also change suitability. New jaundice, significant abdominal symptoms or other suspected adverse effects need medical advice rather than being accepted as an inevitable part of treatment.

Mention migraine, epilepsy, diabetes, high blood pressure, endometriosis, fibroids and any relevant medicine or supplement. These conditions do not all mean the same thing or automatically require the same decision. The clinician may choose a different preparation, arrange monitoring or seek specialist advice. HRT is not a weight-loss treatment, and a new symptom should not automatically be blamed on hormones.

Who needs to avoid a product or obtain specialist advice?

Systemic product labels can contain firm contraindications. For example, the current Bijuva label lists unexplained genital bleeding, breast cancer or its history, oestrogen-dependent cancer, previous or active deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, stroke or heart attack, liver disease, known thrombophilic disorders and product hypersensitivity. These are reasons not to start that product, not simply minor side-effect warnings. Another product or a specialist clinical pathway requires its own assessment.

Local treatment has different exposure and risks, but it still has product-specific restrictions. After breast cancer, nonhormonal vaginal products are usually considered first; persistent symptoms may justify a specialist discussion of low-dose vaginal oestrogen, particularly carefully during aromatase-inhibitor treatment. The effect on recurrence is uncertain. Possible pregnancy, new unexplained bleeding or a serious previous reaction must be reported before prescribing; do not copy someone else’s prescription.

Alternatives when HRT is unsuitable or unwanted

Menopause-specific CBT and selected nonhormonal prescription medicines can help vasomotor symptoms. Options may include particular antidepressants, gabapentin or neurokinin-targeted medicines where approved; indications, interactions and monitoring differ. A medicine used for hot flushes is not automatically the best treatment for depression, and local guidance does not recommend every option as first-line therapy. Ask what the proposed treatment targets and how benefit will be reviewed.

Ordinary soy foods can be nutritious, but soy extracts, purified pollen, black cohosh and acupuncture are not established equivalents to HRT. Some black-cohosh preparations have shown benefit in studies, yet effectiveness and product quality vary; rare liver-injury reports have uncertain causality and still warrant caution. Bring supplement labels for review. Healthy eating, suitable activity and comfort measures can support wellbeing without becoming a prerequisite for effective symptom treatment.

Follow-up, duration and bleeding advice

Agree on the lowest effective dose for the chosen goal, a review after about three months and at least annual review thereafter, sooner for problems. There is no universal one-, two- or five-year limit: ongoing symptoms, risks and preferences guide continuation. If stopping is appropriate, discuss gradual reduction or stopping at once; either approach may be followed by returning symptoms. Do not change a prescribed regimen solely to reach an online hormone target.

Spotting can occur during the first six months of systemic HRT or within three months of changing its dose or preparation. Tell the prescriber about the pattern, and seek prompt advice for unscheduled bleeding beyond those periods. Heavy, prolonged or otherwise concerning bleeding needs earlier assessment; the timelines are not instructions to wait. Bleeding after established menopause outside an expected treatment pattern should be checked even if small or only once.

Prepare a useful discussion and recognise urgent symptoms

Bring your main symptom goals, period and bleeding history, whether you have a uterus, previous operations, personal and family cancer or clot history, medicines, supplements, smoking history and past hormone reactions. Ask whether treatment is systemic or local, what protects the womb, which risks apply to you, whether contraception is still needed and when to return. You can choose not to take HRT or revisit that choice as your needs change.

Get urgent same-day assessment for a newly painful or swollen leg. Chest pain, breathlessness, coughing blood, fainting or loss of consciousness, or sudden stroke-like weakness, facial or speech changes require immediate emergency help, even if neurological symptoms stop. Heavy bleeding with faintness, chest pain or breathing difficulty also needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself or wait for a routine HRT review. Breathing difficulty or throat swelling after a medicine is another emergency.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Take your symptoms, bleeding history, operations and medicine list to the prescriber; ask what each treatment is intended to improve.

Check whether the product is local or systemic, how any womb protection is provided and which personal risks or interactions require another choice.

Agree on follow-up, contraception where needed and a clear plan for bleeding or adverse symptoms; seek urgent care when warning signs occur.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you organise symptom and bleeding notes and questions for an appointment. It cannot decide whether HRT is suitable, compare a personal cancer or clot risk, choose a dose or monitor treatment safety. App records must not delay clinical assessment or emergency care.

When to seek help

Do not start, combine, omit protective hormones or change HRT using someone else’s regimen. Report unexplained or concerning bleeding and review product-specific contraindications. New leg pain or swelling needs urgent same-day assessment. Chest pain, breathlessness, coughing blood, fainting or loss of consciousness, stroke signs, serious allergy or heavy bleeding with faintness or breathing difficulty need immediate emergency help; do not drive yourself.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Choose HRT for a defined symptom or health indication after an individual benefit–risk discussion.
  • Systemic and low-dose local treatment have different roles; route, formulation, timing and personal history change risks.
  • A uterus generally needs progestogen protection with systemic oestrogen; HRT itself is not contraception.
  • Updated warning labels do not mean every medicine is risk-free or that HRT should be used to prevent heart disease or dementia.
  • Review treatment regularly and report unexpected bleeding or serious symptoms promptly.

Frequently asked questions

What are the main benefits of menopausal HRT?

Systemic HRT is highly effective for troublesome hot flushes and night sweats and can reduce bone loss and fractures while used. Local vaginal treatment helps genitourinary symptoms. Sleep or menopause-associated low mood may improve, but depression, urinary problems and other conditions can need separate care.

Can it prevent osteoporosis or keep muscles strong?

It can protect bone while taken, but whether it is the right option depends on fracture risk and the overall balance of benefit and harm. Nutrition, suitable activity and other osteoporosis treatments may be needed. Muscle benefits have limited evidence and should not be promised as complete prevention of ageing-related loss.

Who is most likely to have a favourable benefit–risk balance?

Suitable symptomatic people younger than 60 or within about ten years after menopause often have a favourable balance if there are no contraindications. These are guides for individual decisions, not guarantees or an automatic rule to start or stop at a particular birthday. Earlier ovarian insufficiency needs a separate replacement plan.

Does oestrogen increase womb-cancer risk?

Unopposed systemic oestrogen increases endometrial-cancer risk if you have a uterus. Appropriate progestogen protection is generally required, with the exact regimen chosen by the prescriber. Low-dose local vaginal treatment and certain specifically licensed combinations have different rules; do not remove or add a component yourself.

Is a patch or vaginal ring always safer than a tablet?

A transdermal route usually has a lower blood-clot-risk profile than oral oestrogen, but other risks and your history still matter. Vaginal rings differ: some provide low-dose local treatment and others systemic treatment. Check the exact product, goal and prescribing precautions.

Do the 2026 FDA warning changes mean HRT has no serious risks?

No. The first approved changes concerned six US products, and warnings elsewhere in the label and contraindications remain. Products and countries differ. Read the current information for the medicine offered rather than assuming every boxed warning was removed or that all formulations have the same safety profile.

Can HRT prevent heart disease, Alzheimer’s or Parkinson’s disease?

HRT should not be started solely for cardiovascular or dementia prevention. Proposed neurological benefits do not establish a reason to prescribe it to prevent Parkinson’s disease either. Appropriate symptom treatment is a different decision from promising protection against future disease.

How long can treatment continue?

There is no fixed duration for everyone. Review symptoms, safety, dose, preparation and preferences after about three months and at least yearly, with earlier assessment for problems. Persistent symptoms may justify continued treatment when benefits still outweigh risks; discuss how to stop rather than changing the regimen independently.

Are natural remedies or compounded hormones a safer alternative?

Not automatically. Ordinary soy food differs from concentrated supplements. Evidence, ingredients and interactions vary across herbal products, and compounded hormones have not been shown safer than suitable regulated medicines. Ask about evidence-based nonhormonal treatment instead of assuming a natural label means low risk.

Which symptoms should not wait for the next appointment?

New leg pain or swelling needs urgent same-day assessment. Chest pain, breathlessness, coughing blood, fainting or loss of consciousness, stroke signs, serious allergy or heavy bleeding with faintness or breathing difficulty need immediate emergency care without driving yourself. Unexpected or persistent bleeding should also be reported promptly; do not wait through a suggested adjustment period when symptoms are concerning.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
